FOR FUNDED-TRADER CHALLENGE ENTRANTS

Will your strategy pass the challenge, and is the fee worth paying?

Enter the firm's rules and your own win rate, reward:risk and risk per trade. The simulator plays the evaluation thousands of times and reports your pass probability, how failed attempts ended, the expected fees to pass, the value of the funded phase and the win rate you need to break even. It runs privately in your browser and uploads nothing.

Challenge rules and your strategy

The simulator assumes every trade risks the same share of the starting balance and that outcomes are independent, so streaks, slippage, fees and news-time rules are not modelled. It does not know any firm's exact rules. Treat it as a way to compare risk settings and rule sets, not as a forecast.

    Common questions

    How do I estimate the chance of passing a prop firm challenge?

    Model the challenge as a random walk with walls: your profit target is the upper wall, the maximum drawdown and the daily loss limit are lower walls, and the time limit is a clock. Each trade moves your balance up by your risk times your reward-to-risk ratio with probability equal to your win rate, and down by your risk otherwise. Run that thousands of times and count how many attempts hit the target first. This calculator does exactly that with your own numbers, and shows how the attempts that fail were ended.

    What is the difference between a static and a trailing drawdown?

    A static drawdown floor is fixed at the starting balance minus the allowed loss, so profit gives you a bigger cushion. A trailing drawdown floor follows your highest balance upward, so the cushion stays the same size and profit you have not locked in can disappear. Many firms stop the trailing floor once it reaches the starting balance. The two rules produce very different pass rates for the same strategy, which is why the calculator lets you choose and says which one it used.

    How much does a prop firm challenge really cost if I need several attempts?

    The expected cost to pass is the fee divided by your pass rate. At a 25% pass rate a $540 fee costs $2,160 on average before you are funded, and any single trader can spend far more or less than the average. This is a simulation of assumed inputs rather than a forecast, so treat it as a way to compare rule sets and risk settings, not as a promise.

    What risk per trade gives the best chance of passing?

    Neither the smallest nor the largest. Very small risk rarely breaches a limit but runs out the clock before reaching the target, and large risk reaches the target faster but breaches a loss limit more often. The table under the result sweeps risk per trade across your own rules so you can see where the pass rate peaks, then check that the peak still survives a losing streak.

    Is passing the challenge worth the fee if my edge is small?

    Only if expected payouts exceed the fee. The calculator estimates that by simulating a funded phase with the same strategy, paying you your profit split each time the account gains your payout target, and ending the account on a breach. If your expectancy per trade is zero or negative, no rule set fixes the odds and the fee is the cost of a ticket, which the calculator states plainly.

    Does the calculator send my numbers anywhere?

    No. The simulation runs in your browser, nothing is uploaded, and there is no account. A share link stores your inputs in the link itself, so send it only to people who may see them. It does not know any firm's exact rules, so enter the rules from the firm's own terms and check them yourself.

vs-a-trading-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Prop Firm Challenge Calculator

Prop Firm Challenge Calculator vs. a trading spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can tell you how many winning trades a profit target needs. It rarely plays the order of wins and losses against a trailing drawdown, a daily loss limit and a time limit at once — which is what this free, private simulator does with your own win rate and risk.

Where a spreadsheet stops being enough

Most challenge entrants already keep a sheet: win rate, average win, average loss, a column that multiplies them. It answers whether the strategy makes money on average. A challenge is not an average; it is a path with walls on both sides and a deadline, and the same win rate passes or fails depending on the sequence.

What you are trying to seeA spreadsheet you build yourselfThis simulator
Trades needed to hit the target.One division, if you assume every trade wins its average.Counts them under your win rate, so the target is reached on a distribution of days, not a single day.
The order of wins and losses.Averages hide it, so a losing streak at the start looks the same as one at the end.Plays thousands of orderings and reports how many end at the target, at a loss limit or at the clock.
A trailing drawdown that follows your high.Needs a running-maximum column per scenario, rebuilt for each setting.Applies a static or trailing floor, with or without the stop at the starting balance.
A daily loss limit that resets each day.Needs a day boundary and a within-day running total.Checks it after every trade, and says when the limit alone ends most failed attempts.
What a fee is worth.Fee times attempts, if you already know the pass rate.Divides the fee by the simulated pass rate and nets it against simulated funded payouts.
The risk per trade that works best.One scenario per column, retyped for each.Sweeps six risk settings under your rules and shows where the pass rate peaks.

A spreadsheet with a random-number column and a few thousand rows can do the same job. This is the version with the rules already written, nothing to rebuild for the next firm, and your numbers kept in your browser.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the simulation runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you enter is uploaded. It is a simulation of assumed inputs, not a forecast.

Common questions

Can't I just model a prop firm challenge in a spreadsheet?

Yes. A spreadsheet is good at the deterministic part: how many winning trades reach the target and how many losses hit the drawdown. What it handles badly is the order of wins and losses, because the same win rate passes or fails depending on the sequence. A simulation plays thousands of sequences against the daily loss limit, the drawdown floor and the clock together, and reports the share that pass.

What does a trading spreadsheet usually leave out of a challenge?

The interaction between rules. A trailing drawdown that rises with your high, a daily loss limit that resets each day, a minimum number of trading days and a time limit all depend on the path your balance takes. Averages cannot show a path, so a sheet built on average win and average loss tends to say the strategy passes whenever its expectancy is positive.

Does the calculator replace backtesting my strategy?

No. It takes a win rate and a reward-to-risk ratio you supply, from a backtest or a journal, and shows what the challenge rules do to them. If those inputs are optimistic the output is optimistic. It is a simulation of assumed inputs, not a forecast, and trading carries a risk of loss.

Ready to run your numbers? Open the Prop Firm Challenge Calculator.
